newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Investors cut through Ukraine's tangled telecom web.
newsitem.headline: Investors cut through Ukraine's tangled telecom web.

text.p: World telecommunications companies are cutting through the tangle of Ukraine's ancient, static-ridden phone system to drag it into the modern era and profit from a predicted boom.
"Demand here is greater than supply," said Oleg Stefanjuk, project manager for Sweden's LM Ericsson International AB.
"People waiting for phones are willing to pay $500, $600 or $1,000, but the infrastructure just isn't there."

Industry analysts estimate that companies like Ericsson, which has invested $30 million in local network and mobile communications since 1994, could bring a badly-needed $500 million to $1 billion in investment in the next few years.
"This country is a target for investment. In terms of potential there are 52 million people and 8 million phones," said Stewart Reich, president of Utel, a European-Ukranian venture.
A better phone system is vital if Ukraine is to succeed in attracting more foreign businesses. Foreign investment since independence in 1991 has been a paltry $1.5 billion.
Some 50 international and local firms displayed switching systems, mobile networks, and pay phones at a recent trade show.

Utel has opened long-distance switches in a string of Ukrainian cities and plans to focus on local network development next year. Utel is owned 51 percent by Ukrtelekom, 19.5 percent by AT&T Corp., 19.5 percent by Deutsche Telekom AG and 10 percent by Dutch PTT.

State-owned monopolist Ukrtelekom, which has launched a $20 billion programme to provide 700,000 to 1 million telephone lines a year to 2005, has demonstrated its willingness to welcome private-sector investment, investors said.

This is considered unusual in a country where investors complain about bureaucratic hurdles, demands for bribes and a lack of legislation -- although they say the sector is so new it has not encountered traditional government interference.

"Ukraine has great potential. It's more attractive than Russia. There is more order here with government programmes and strategies," said Leonid Berkovich of Schlumberger Industries S.A., hoping to sell 200,000 pay phones to Ukraine.

Scattered investment to date in the Soviet-era phone system has created a bizarre hybrid -- Utel's development of long-distance communications has made it easier to call North America than make a local call.
While nouveau riche Ukrainians flaunt their expensive mobile phones in cities, villages with populations of a several thousand typically have only one telephone -- manufactured in the 1950s.

Local pay phones, at least those that work, are free because the old karbovanets currency withdrawn in September consisted only of paper money so there were no coins to insert. They stand next to new long-distance pay phones requiring cards.
In November Ukraine, in partnership with Italy, Turkey and Russia, launched the ITUR fiber-optic cable under the Black Sea to wean the country from long-distance dependency on satellites.

"I think it's going to be incredible," said Gregory Perchatsch of Motorola Inc., who said Motorola would invest $120 million in a nationwide mobile phone system, in addition to similar investments from other mobile companies.
"It could go up to $240 million. That's a quarter of a billion of direct investment in two to three years," he said.

U.S. communications company Qualcomm Inc. announced last month that it planned to start producing equipment for its CDMA digital cellular system in mid-1997, the country's first wireless local system, hoping eventually to invest $2 billion.
"It's a large country and a large and attractive market," Chief Executive Irwin Jacobs said.
